Death Matters

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Space for traditional burials is fast running out, but besides cremation, what are the alternatives?

Unique Selling Point:
It is estimated that there are about 25,000 burials in Johannesburg per annum, and space is fast running out. Not only do burials take up space, but cemeteries are often dead space and costly to maintain. On top of that is the environmental footprint of a traditional burial. Bodies are embalmed with formaldehyde and coffins are made of wood (a precious resource) and often lacquered and glued that end up leaching into the soil. Coffins are also very often lined with plastic which slows down the decomposition of the body. But what are the alternatives and are they viable options for the future?

Summary:
In South Africa, a new trend of eco burials is emerging. This means that the body is not embalmed, often wrapped in cloth and buried in a wicker or paper mache coffin. This makes the actual burial a lot more environmental friendly, but it does not solve the space problem. Cremation solves the space problem, but it has a huge environmental footprint. It takes about 15KWH of electricity to cremate one body. Besides the smoke pumped into the atmosphere, greenhouse gases are also released, not to mention toxic formaldehyde from the embalming process and other chemicals used in the making and varnishing of the coffin. Every body is cremated in a wood coffin, once again using a great deal of wood. Internationally there are some alternatives emerging...

Further information:
Since the beginning of time we have dealt with dead bodies in a variety of ways:
Ancient tribes of Papua New Guinea and the Wari People of Brazil practiced endocannabalism -- they ate the dead.
People of Nepal would leave dead bodies on a cliff for the vultures to feed on -- sky burial. (Incidentally this has lead to a 95% crash in the vulture population of India, because vultures are very sensitive to anti-inflammatory medicines used by humans)
There are current experiments with Infinity Mushrooms, whereby dead bodies are dressed in a fungal suit and the mushrooms basically digest the entire body.
In Seattle Katrina Spade is spearheading the Urban Death Project -- A 3-story composting station is being built in the city. It will be able to compost about 60 bodies at a time over a period of 6-8 weeks. Family members can then get some compost as a symbolic gesture.
Resumation / Aquamation is also known as a water cremation. Bodies are heated in an extreme alkali solution. Through a process of alkaline hydrolysis the body is reduced to a liquid which can basically just be flushed down the drain.
Promession is currently being tested in Germany. This is when a body is frozen in liquid nitrogen. It is then vibrated until it shatters. The powder that is left over can be scattered or buried.

All these have a far lesser environmental footprint, but there are also of course tradition and perceptions to deal with. Would you really be content to simply flush your mother's remains down the drain? We will look at all these aspects , including costs and feasibility.

Script:


DEATH MATTERS




V/O
Through the ages humans have adopted various practices to memorialise loved ones after death... from the cremations on the banks of the Ganges to the sky burials in Tibet where bodies are simply left for scavenging vultures...

South Africans are still traditional – opting for a conventional burial in a cemetery... But for how long will this stay sustainable?

LINK
Land is the burning issue in South Africa and even cemeteries are running out of space. Along with burgeoning populations we're going to have to look at alternatives to burial when our loved ones depart.
V/O
Jenny Moodley is the spokesperson for Joburg City Parks which manages the cemeteries in Johannesburg.
Jenny Moodley
There are 38 cemeteries across the city of Johannesburg. Unfortunately 34 are dormant, meaning they've reached full capacity for primary burials and only four are active.
V/O
Besides the space issue, traditional burials also have a large ecological footprint. Varnish and glue used in coffins and the chemicals used to embalm bodies leach into the ground. So now people are increasingly looking for greener alternatives.
Sonja Smith
I use the sea grass, the coco-stick and the loom. It's beautiful. It looks like a natural moses basket, if I can call it that.
V/O
Sonja Smith founded a funeral group that specialises in alternative funerals because trends are slowly changing.
Sonja Smith
If I show the coffins and the woven baskets, the family, the daughter would say, for me one day, I want the green burial, but for my mom now, let's go the traditional way.
V/O
Cremation is the primary alternative to burial, but it's not always a viable option.
LINK
There is cultural and religious opposition to cremation but it is being utilised more often. Apart from being cost-effective there are endless ideas of how to scatter or even keep the ashes.
V/O
Ashes can be interred in memorial walls that take up less space… or be scattered at a place of meaning…
Sonja
You can also when you scatter ashes on the beach, you can pick up shells or rocks from that specific place and bring that back in the container that you used to scatter the ashes...

Then there is artwork that brings beauty from ashes.
Lianne
There's people that will actually take some of a loved one's ashes and include it into paint and actually do a painting with the ashes in the painting.
V/O
Funeral director, Lianne Barlon, says there are many creative ways to immortalise a beloved's ashes. One example is glass moulded around the ashes to form unique artwork or even jewellery.
Lianne
DEREK: Look at this, a ring, now that's incredible to wear that all the time as a reminder.

LIANNE: Yes.

Lianne
My eldest son passed away 11 years ago, and I actually scattered his ashes at sea and I wish that I had known about something like this because I would have loved to have something so beautiful that I could have kept.

DEREK: And that is with you all the time...

Absolutely.
V/O
More than just biodigradable, this pod literally brings life from death.... For Christo Cilliers it is a way of giving back to the earth even after your life.
Chris
We're trying to create an emphasis on celebrating life by leaving behind a living memorial that creates a natural habitat for other forms of life.
V/O
The urn comes with three indigenous tree seeds so it can be planted virtually anywhere.
Chris
We've had customers who've planted their biotree urns in nature reserves, all across the country.


V/O
Possibly the biggest way of giving back is donating your body to science. Professor Hoosen Vawda heads the Body Donor Foundation of South Africa. Only about 15 to 25 people a year bequeath their bodies to universities.
Prof Hoosen Vawda
If you donate your body you are actually leaving a legacy behind in terms of ensuring that the healthcare professionals that are being trained in whichever field in SA will be empowered on a hands-on basis and therefore they'll be able to handle any medical condition....
V/O
After serving the medical profession, the body is cremated and the ashes are returned to the family.

Internationally there are even more radical trends emerging. In the States a company in Seattle is working on a process to speed up the decomposition of human remains. The body is placed in a hexagonal pod, covered in wood chips and aerated.
LINK
And in about 30 days you'll end up with nothing but rich compost, like this, which you can then use to plant a symbolic tree or just scatter.
V/O
In Sweden “promession” was developed by Susanne Wiigh-Mäsak (weegh-messiek)– The body is frozen in liquid nitrogen. Then the crystallised body is vibrated and disintegrated.
LINK
Well we haven't got a body to demonstrate the process but let's see what happens when we dip a rose into liquid nitrogen at minus 196 degrees centigrade.
V/O
The left-over particles are freeze-dried and can then be buried or scattered.
LINK
Another method of body disposal is ressumation or aquamation which is considered to be more environmentally friendly than cremation is being considered by the private sector in South Africa. The corpse is virtually melted in a strong alkaline solution. Now our goldfish – don't worry, it's origami – is about to experience a similar fate.
V/O
This process reduces the body to approximately 2% of its original weight. It is already in use in 16 States in America, in Canada and the UK...

South Africa may still be a long way from accepting alternative methods, according to Dr Tsepang Leoota, a specialist in sustainable urban planning at the University of the Witwatersrand.
Dr Tsepang Leuta
If we're talking cremation and people still feel that when you burn, or when you cremate a body it can still feel pain, what more when we introduce a process that liquifies the body and we have to drain the liquid or we have to flush it down the toilet. So that still sounds a bit far fetched for South Africans to come to terms with.
V/O
Unlike some other big cities, Joburg still has space for burials for the foreseeable future, but City Parks is nonetheless urging residents to consider burial alternatives.
Jenny Moodley
We don't want future generations to be bearing this burden of managing dormant cemeteries, so for us it is largely an education process...
V/O
Where cemeteries have reached capacity, family members are requested to consider sharing graves.
Dr Tsepang Leuta
At the rate that people are dying, at the rate that we need to find spaces for burial it's not really sustainable in the long term.
V/o
After death options are about personal choice and belief, and there is no one-size-fits-al solution for the future.
Dr Tsepang Leuta
South Africa is quite diverse, we have people of different cultures and beliefs, hence we need to find multiple solutions, not just one blanket solution but in doing that we also need to be sensitive to people's cultures and religions. We need to respond to our local needs.


PROMO 10”
From freezing bodies in liquid nitrogen to paintings and artwork made from a deceased ashes, people are looking for alternative methods to memorialize their loved ones...


PROMO 15”




Traditionally liquid nitrogen is used as an industrial coolant, or during some medical procedures ... now a new technique where the deceased are frozen this way, could change how people bury their loved ones in the future...



PROMO 15”
All over the world people are coming up with alternatives to traditional burial. From freezing the deceased to memorialising a loved one's ashes...


UPSOUND CHRIS
by leaving behind a living memorial we're trying to create an emphasis on celebrating life ….



PROMO 30”
All over the world land for cemeteries is becoming scarcer and people are developing new and greener options to dispose of the deceased. Bodies can even be composted or frozen in liquid nitrogen...


But here in South Africa we seem to be clinging to the traditional ways...

UPSOUND SONJA
If I show the coffins and the woven baskets, the family, the daughter would say, for me one day, I want the green burial, but for my mom now, let's go the traditional way.

In Seattle Katrina Spade is spearheading the Urban Death Project -- A 3-story composting station is being built in the city. It will be able to compost about 60 bodies at a time over a period of 6-8 weeks. Family members can then get some compost as a symbolic gesture. Resumation / Aquamation is also known as a water cremation. Bodies are heated in an extreme alkali solution. Through a process of alkaline hydrolysis the body is reduced to a liquid which can basically just be flushed down the drain. Promession is currently being tested in Germany. This is when a body is frozen in liquid nitrogen. It is then vibrated until it shatters. The powder that is left over can be scattered or buried. All these have a far lesser environmental footprint, but there are also of course tradition and perceptions to deal with. Would you really be content to simply flush your mother's remains down the drain? We will look at all these aspects , including costs and feasibility.
